references.text: In [ref:Matt 23:13|Matthew 23:13], Jesus pronounces the parallel woe against the scribes and Pharisees: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. You neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in." This is the closest parallel to Luke 11:52.

In [ref:Isa 22:22|Isaiah 22:22], it speaks of the key to the house of David being placed on Eliakim's shoulder—"he shall open, and none shall shut; he shall shut, and none shall open." The motif of the key that opens and shuts is the background for the image of "the key of knowledge" in Luke 11:52.

In [ref:Matt 23:4|Matthew 23:4], Jesus accuses the scribes of tying up heavy burdens and laying them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with a finger. This shows the same accusation: the legalists hinder others without practicing what they require.

In [ref:Rev 3:7|Revelation 3:7], Christ is described as the one who has "the key of David, he who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens." The key motif here is linked to messianic authority, in contrast to the legalists who have taken away the key of knowledge.

In [ref:Matt 23:29-32|Matthew 23:29-32], Jesus accuses the scribes and Pharisees of building the tombs of the prophets and thus filling up their fathers' measure. This context is part of the same sequence of woes that parallels Luke 11:47-52, where the legalists prevent people from coming to the truth.

In [ref:Hos 4:6|Hosea 4:6], God says: "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge." The priests have rejected knowledge, and therefore God will reject them. This is an Old Testament parallel to the accusation that the legalists have taken away the key of knowledge, thereby depriving the people of access to God's truth.

In [ref:Matt 15:14|Matthew 15:14], Jesus calls the Pharisees "blind guides of the blind," and says that both will fall into a pit. This corresponds with the accusation in Luke 11:52 that the legalists neither enter the kingdom of God themselves nor allow others to enter.

In [ref:Rom 2:19-20|Romans 2:19-20], Paul describes Jews who are convinced that they are guides for the blind, a light for those in darkness, instructors of the foolish, and teachers of infants. This self-understanding reveals the same problem Jesus addresses: those who should convey knowledge fail in their task.

In [ref:Luk 11:42-44|Luke 11:42-44], Jesus pronounces woes against the Pharisees in the same discourse. The context shows that the accusations against the Pharisees and the legalists belong together: both groups fail in their calling and mislead the people.
